conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that denosumab substantially reduces the risk of vertebral fractures in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis during treatment, supported by randomized controlled trials.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
The evidence does not support "no" — denosumab does reduce vertebral fracture risk in osteoporosis; the answer should be revised to "yes."

**Conclusion:** The randomized, placebo-controlled evidence clearly shows denosumab reduces vertebral fracture risk while on treatment. The initial premise (that the answer is "no") is incorrect.

**Evidence:** The pivotal FREEDOM trial, a large randomized controlled trial in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, found that denosumab given subcutaneously every 6 months for 36 months reduced new radiographic vertebral fractures from 7.2% (placebo) to 2.3% (denosumab)—a 68% relative risk reduction (p<0.001), along with reductions in nonvertebral and hip fractures (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493). This finding has been consistently replicated: a 10-year FREEDOM Extension study confirmed sustained low rates of vertebral fracture and progressive BMD gains with continued therapy (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8799550/).

There is an important caveat, however: this fracture-risk reduction is contingent on continued treatment. Multiple analyses show that *discontinuing* denosumab produces a rebound increase in bone turnover and a loss of BMD gains, which can lead to an increased risk of multiple vertebral fractures shortly after stopping—sometimes exceeding what would have occurred without any treatment (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3617467/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5915244/). This is why guidelines recommend transitioning promptly to another antiresorptive agent if denosumab is stopped.

**Bottom line:** While on denosumab, vertebral fracture risk is substantially reduced. The nuance is not whether denosumab works (it clearly does), but that stopping it abruptly can cause rebound vertebral fractures—so the original "no" answer is inaccurate.
